prompt: A team asks "MongoDB or Cassandra?" for a new service. What should be answered first?

choices.text: Which of the two has the better benchmark
choices.why: A benchmark measures somebody else's workload; the question is about yours.

choices.text: The operations and their costs
choices.why: Right. The access pattern decides; the brand follows.

choices.text: Which one the team has used before
choices.why: Familiarity is a tie-breaker, not the first question.

choices.text: Which licence is cheaper
choices.why: Both are free to run for your own application; the licence is a later line of the record.

prompt: Match each access pattern to the family that fits it.

pairs.left: a whole order with varying attributes, read and written as one
billions of sensor readings appended, read by device and time range
a session looked up by its token, with an expiry
stock, orders and payments changed together in one transaction

prompt: A founder says: "we will have a billion events a day, so we need Cassandra now". Today the shop has ten thousand a day. What does the lesson say to write down?

choices.text: Nothing: forecasts do not belong in a decision record
choices.why: They belong there, labelled as forecasts.

choices.text: MongoDB, as a compromise between the two
choices.why: A compromise between a fact and a guess is still a guess.

choices.text: Cassandra, since migrating later is impossible
choices.why: Migration costs a project; Cassandra now costs every query written first, from today.

choices.text: The forecast, labelled as one
choices.why: Right. A pattern you might have is a revisit trigger, not today's design.

prompt: Why does the lesson say the table classifies operations, not systems?

choices.text: Systems are too large to classify
choices.why: Size is not the reason; mixed patterns are.

choices.text: Each operation needs its own database
choices.why: Most operations of most systems share one relational database.

choices.text: Families are defined by their operations, not by vendors
choices.why: True in a sense, but it does not explain why a whole system is the wrong unit.

choices.text: One application has many operations, fitting different families
choices.why: Right. The shop's orders fit Postgres while its page views fit Redis.

prompt: The plan for `doc @> '{"gift": {"wrap": true}}'` showed `Bitmap Index Scan on orders_doc`. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The GIN index found the rows
choices.why: Right. 2,000 of 100,000 orders were found through the index.

choices.text: Postgres converted the JSON to columns
choices.why: The column stays `jsonb`; the index covers its contents.

choices.text: The query was sent to MongoDB
choices.why: Only Postgres was involved.

choices.text: Every row was read and then filtered
choices.why: That would be a Seq Scan, which the plan did not show.

prompt: After `docker kill postgres` and `docker start postgres`, how many rows did the unlogged `cache` table hold?
Why did `page_views` keep its row after the crash while `cache` lost its own?

choices.text: `page_views` has a primary key and `cache` does not
choices.why: Both have one; persistence is the difference.

choices.text: The upsert wrote `cache` to memory only
choices.why: Unlogged tables have data files; they just skip the log.

choices.text: `cache` had expired
choices.why: Its expiry was five minutes away; the crash emptied it.

choices.text: `cache` is unlogged: no write-ahead log, so recovery empties it
choices.why: Right. `relpersistence` said `u`; recovery replayed the log for `p` tables only.

prompt: A worker held job 1 with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` while a second worker ran the same query. What did the second get, and why?

choices.text: Nothing until the first committed
choices.why: That is `FOR UPDATE` without `SKIP LOCKED`, which queues.

choices.text: Job 2, skipping the locked row
choices.why: Right, and without waiting.

choices.text: An error about a lock conflict
choices.why: That is `NOWAIT`; `SKIP LOCKED` simply passes over.

choices.text: Job 1, since reads are not blocked
choices.why: `FOR UPDATE` is a locking read; it does not hand out a locked row.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson name as things Postgres does not do as well? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Sorted sets and streams at memory speed
choices.why: Right: that is what Redis is.

choices.text: Accepting writes on many machines at once
choices.why: Right: one primary takes every write.

choices.text: Accepting writes in two regions at once
choices.why: Right: that is Cassandra's multi-datacentre replication.

choices.text: Indexing JSON documents
choices.why: The GIN index on `jsonb` did exactly that.

choices.text: Atomic upserts
choices.why: `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` is one.

prompt: In Postgres, `INSERT ... ON ___ DO UPDATE` turns an insert into an upsert.
Which sign says an operation belongs in Redis beside the main database?

choices.text: It stores the only copy of the customer's payments, which must never be lost
choices.why: Payments are the least forgivable data the shop has.

choices.text: Its queries are not known yet
choices.why: Unknown queries argue for a relational database.

choices.text: It is small, hot and forgivable
choices.why: Right. Lessons 13 and 15 showed what Redis can lose; an operation that can afford it fits.

choices.text: It changes several entities that have to agree
choices.why: That is the relational row of the table.

prompt: A product catalogue stores monitors and cables with different attributes, but every product is also joined to stock, prices and orders in reports. Where does the lesson lean?

choices.text: Cassandra, for the reports
choices.why: Ad-hoc reports are what a query-first model handles worst.

choices.text: Postgres, with the varying attributes in a `jsonb` column
choices.why: Right. The documents are one table among many, not the whole application.

choices.text: Redis, as a cache of the catalogue
choices.why: A cache may sit in front, but it is not where the catalogue lives.

choices.text: MongoDB, because the shapes vary
choices.why: Varying shape alone is what a `jsonb` column handles; the joins argue the other way.

prompt: Which case is the strongest for Cassandra?

choices.text: A shop's orders, payments and stock
choices.why: They change together in transactions; that is relational.

choices.text: Device telemetry in two regions
choices.why: Right: write volume, a known query, and more than one datacentre.

choices.text: Sessions with a thirty-minute expiry
choices.why: Small, hot and forgivable: Redis.

choices.text: A dashboard whose questions change weekly
choices.why: Changing questions are what Cassandra charges for most.

prompt: A Redis structure that keeps a ranking ordered as scores change is a sorted ___.
The shop commits a sale in Postgres and then sets the new stock in Redis. The process dies between the two. What does the product page show?

choices.text: An error, because the transaction rolled back
choices.why: The commit had already happened.

choices.text: Nothing, because Redis evicts keys it cannot confirm
choices.why: Redis does not know the key is stale.

choices.text: The old stock: Redis never heard of the sale
choices.why: Right. That is the dual write's gap, and no retry closes it because the retrying process died.

choices.text: The new stock, because Postgres pushes changes to Redis
choices.why: Nothing connects them unless you build it.

prompt: Put the transactional outbox in order, for one sale.
items: Insert the order and an outbox row
The relay reads the outbox row
The relay sets the stock in Redis
The relay marks the row done
trap: Marking before applying would lose the entry if the relay died in between.

prompt: Why must an outbox entry say "set the stock of MN-330 to 0" rather than "decrement the stock of MN-330"?

choices.text: Decrements are not supported by Redis
choices.why: `DECR` exists; repeating it is the problem.

choices.text: A dead relay repeats its last entry
choices.why: Right. A relay that dies after the SET and before marking repeats it.

choices.text: Absolute values use less space in the outbox
choices.why: Size is not the concern; repetition is.

choices.text: Postgres cannot store negative numbers in jsonb
choices.why: It can, and it is irrelevant here.

prompt: Which of these is a cost of running Redis beside Postgres even when nothing fails?

choices.text: Licences forbid using both together
choices.why: No licence discussed in lesson 21 does.

choices.text: Two backups and two restore drills to keep
choices.why: Right, with two skills on call and two places for access to be wrong.

choices.text: Postgres becomes slower because Redis exists
choices.why: Redis takes load off Postgres if anything.

choices.text: Transactions stop working in Postgres
choices.why: They work as before; they just do not reach Redis.

prompt: What belongs in the "revisit when" paragraph of a decision record?

choices.text: The date of the next major version
choices.why: A release is not a reason to change databases by itself.

choices.text: Nothing: decisions are final
choices.why: The record exists so a later reader knows when it stops holding.

choices.text: A number or an event, such as writes outgrowing the largest primary
choices.why: Right. Something that can be noticed, not a feeling.

choices.text: "When the team feels ready"
choices.why: A feeling cannot be noticed by anyone else.

prompt: In the shop's record, why did MongoDB lose for the orders even though an order is an aggregate?

choices.text: It changes with stock and payment
choices.why: Right. The aggregate is not the unit of change; the transaction is.

choices.text: The volume is too high
choices.why: The volume was thousands a day, low for any of them.

choices.text: MongoDB's licence forbids shops
choices.why: The SSPL restricts offering MongoDB as a service, not using it.

choices.text: MongoDB cannot store arrays of items
choices.why: It does, in lesson 6.

prompt: A team keeps a leaderboard for a game in Postgres, recomputed with `ORDER BY score` on every page view, and it is now slow. What does this course suggest?

choices.text: Move the whole game to Cassandra
choices.why: The problem is one structure, not the write volume of the whole game.

choices.text: A sorted set in Redis beside Postgres, fed through an outbox
choices.why: Right: a memory-speed structure for one hot operation, and no dual write.

choices.text: Make the scores table UNLOGGED
choices.why: That makes writes cheaper and loses the scores in a crash; the slow part is the ranking read.

choices.text: Store the scores in a `jsonb` column with a GIN index
choices.why: GIN answers containment, not ordering by a number.

prompt: Which of these did this lesson actually run in the lab? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `SKIP LOCKED` handing two workers different jobs
choices.why: Right: the second worker got job 2.

choices.text: A GIN index answering a containment query
choices.why: Right: the Bitmap Index Scan.

choices.text: An unlogged table emptied by a crash
choices.why: Right: `docker kill`, then a count of 0.

choices.text: A relay copying outbox rows into Redis
choices.why: The lesson says plainly it does not build the relay.
